newsitem.title: CROATIA: First U.S. troops to leave former Yugoslavia.
newsitem.headline: First U.S. troops to leave former Yugoslavia.

text.p: The first batch of U.S. soldiers sent to Bosnia as peacekeepers a year ago will start withdrawing on Wednesday in line with orders from the Pentagon, a U.S. army official said.

"This is the first official withdrawal of American troops from Bosnia as part of the redeployment process to the central region (Germany and Hungary)," U.S. Army spokesman Colonel Larry Icenogel said by telephone from Tuzla.
Tuzla airbase in northern Bosnia is the headquarters of the 15,000-strong U.S. force serving currently in Bosnia as part of the NATO-led implementation force (IFOR).
Peacekeeping in Bosnia is NATO's largest military operation since the alliance was created.
Some 60,000 international peacekeepers were stationed in Bosnia after the warring parties signed a peace accord last December, ending 3-1/2 years of Bosnian war.
U.S. President Bill Clinton had promised a hostile Republican-doiminated Congress he would pull out the U.S. forces after a year.
Icenogel said the first two U.S. units, which have already left northern Bosnia, would set off from Slavonski Brod, Croatia, at 0700 local time (0500 gmt).
"There is an executive order to commence their withdrawal ...(it comes) from the Pentagon, through the U.S. European Command in Stuttgart (Germany)..., and then on to us," Icenogel said.
The units, the Headquarters battery division and 127 Military Police Company with up to 100 soldiers would be divided in five convoys.
Slavonski Brod, linked with Bosnia by a bridge over the Sava river, is to serve as a staging base for the withdrawal for the U.S. troops.
The first of some 5,000 U.S. troops sent to cover the withdrawal left Germany for Bosnia on Tuesday and some of those might stay on until March next year, the Pentagon said last week.
IFOR's mandate in Bosnia terminates on December 20.
But NATO, ignoring Republicans' protests, has been pushing for a follow-on force with a U.S. presence to remain in Bosnia after December.
The U.S. pullout date has already slipped by weeks due to a postponement of municipal elections, now set for late November.
"The redeployment process will carry on regardless of whether there is a follow-on force," Icenogel said.
But he maintained some of the troops would stay to provide a secure environment for the voting.
"But immediately after the elections, withdrawal of the troops will pick up," Icenogel said.
"We will keep drawing out until as many U.S. soldiers are out of Bosnia as possible (by December)," he said.
